podcast.body: Brian Wilson drew direct inspiration from this song, specifically its melody and the opening verse's distinctive recitation of place names, which he subsequently adapted for The Beach Boys' "Surfin' USA." Due to the pronounced similarities, Chuck Berry was awarded the sole songwriting credit for "Surfin' USA," a decision that proved financially advantageous for him as "Surfin' USA" became a perennial oldies hit, unlike "Sweet Little Sixteen" itself. "Brian Wilson had been inspired by Chuck Berry's sweet little 16, and in particular the opening verse, which had just listed a lot of places."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 117: "Don't Worry Baby" by the Beach Boys

podcast.body: Recorded at the same session as "Real in a Rockin'," this song captured the experience of being a rock and roll fan, moving beyond just dancing to music to describe fandom as a major part of life. While it contains elements of the "teen girl fan filtered through the male gaze," its strength lies in verses where the girl becomes the viewpoint character, expressing excitement for shows and her collections. The song famously name-checks "American Bandstand" and its location, Philadelphia. "Sweet Little Sixteen was one of the first songs about the experience of being a rock and roll fan."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 67: "Johnny B. Goode", by Chuck Berry

podcast.body: The melody of this song was entirely lifted by The Beach Boys for their 1963 song "Surfin' U.S.A." After intervention from Chuck Berry's music publisher, Berry was added to the songwriting credits for "Surfin' U.S.A." in 1966. "However, the melody was lifted entirely from a 1958 Chuck Berry song entitled Sweet Little X-D."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
